sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Amaterasu** ​(*amaterasu*) — ‌Sun Goddess, ‌Shintō ​— belongs ​to ​the Japanese ​tradition. The ​name ‌means "Sun ​goddess ​in Shinto"[^1].

‌Amaterasu is ​the ‌sun itself ​made kami ‌— ​the great ​august ​kami who ​illuminates heaven ​and ‌the ancestor ​of ‌the imperial ​house. Her ‌withdrawal ​into the ‌Heavenly ​Rock Cave ‌and her ​restoration ​by dance ‌and persuasion ‌form ‌the central ​crisis ​of Shinto ‌cosmology.

PuniCodex ​restores ​the name ‌as ​**Amaterasu**. The ​plain ASCII ‌form ​*amaterasu* is ‌the modern ​Hepburn ​romanization; the ​restoration ​capitalizes the ‌conventional spelling. ‌Because ​the Japanese ‌source ​script uses ​logographic characters ‌whose ‌distinctive visual ‌form cannot ‌be ​conveyed in ‌the ​basic Latin ​alphabet, and ​because ‌no diacritic ​or ​special letter ​is added ‌in ​this restoration, ​the ​name is ‌placed in ​Tier ‌2. The ​Unicode form ‌remains ​the philologically ‌complete ‌reference, while ​the ASCII ​spelling ​is a ​practical ‌convenience for ‌the domain-name ​system[^2].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in Japanese ‌characters as ​**天照**. Etymologically it ​means "Sun ​goddess in ​Shinto"[^1].

The ​name is ‌usually analyzed as ​*ama-terasu*, "shining ​in heaven," ‌from *ama* ​(heaven) and *terasu* ‌(to shine, ​to illuminate). ‌The fuller ​cult name ​is *Amaterasu-ōmikami*, "the ​great august ​kami who ​illuminates heaven." ‌She is the ​ancestral kami ‌(*sojin*) of ​the imperial ‌house and the ​central deity ‌of the ​Shinto pantheon.

‌The ASCII ​form *amaterasu* survives ​only because ‌the early ‌domain-name system ‌could not carry ​Japanese characters ​or diacritics; ‌it is ​a technological ​compromise, not an ‌ancient spelling. ​The Unicode ​restoration **Amaterasu** ‌gives the conventional ​Hepburn romanization ‌with initial ​capitalization, the ​standard scholarly way ​to cite ​a proper ‌name in ‌romanized Japanese. ​The name is ‌Tier 2 ​because the ​restoration does ‌not add a ‌distinctive diacritic ‌or special ‌letter absent ​from the ‌ASCII form.

The ​letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- ​**a** → ‌**A** — Same
​- **m** ​→ **m** ​— Same
‌- **a** → ​**a** — ​Same
- ​**t** → ‌**t** — ​Same
- **e** ‌→ **e** ​— Same
‌- **r** ​→ **r** — ‌Same
- ‌**a** → ​**a** — ​Same
- ​**s** → **s** ​— Same
‌- **u** ‌→ **u** ​— Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The conventional ​reading of ‌the name ‌is **/a.ma.te.ɾa.sɯ/** ​— Modern ​Japanese (Standard ​Japanese)[^1].

For ​the modern speaker, ​the closest ‌approximation is: ​'AMATERASU' — ​pronounce each ‌vowel clearly ​and avoid ‌English diphthongs. Japanese ​is mora-timed, ‌so each ​syllable receives ​roughly equal ​weight.



Amaterasu ​is Tier 2 ​because the ‌ASCII form ​*amaterasu* already ‌represents the ​same phonemic ‌sequence; no ​stress mark, length ‌mark, or ​distinctive letter ‌is required ​to recover ​the spoken ‌name.

Japanese ‌is a mora-timed ‌language: each ​short syllable ​receives roughly ‌equal temporal ​weight, and ​long vowels ‌or double consonants ​count as ​separate morae. ‌The name ​**Amaterasu** therefore ‌falls into ​a regular rhythmic ​pattern that ​is lost ​if an ‌English speaker ‌stresses one ​syllable heavily[^2]. ‌The Hepburn romanization ​used here ​records the ‌modern standard ‌pronunciation; it ‌does not ‌preserve the ​historical pitch accent ‌of the ​word, which ​differs across ​dialects. When ‌reading the ​name aloud, ​keep the vowels ​pure and ‌avoid English ​diphthongs: the ​restoration **Amaterasu** ​is the ‌conventional scholarly citation ​form, not ‌a phonetic ​transcription with ‌added diacritics. ​Because the ‌ASCII string ‌*amaterasu* already encodes ​the same ​phonemic sequence, ​the name ​remains Tier ‌2 in ‌the PuniCodex ​system.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌written ​in ​Japanese ​characters ​as ​**天照** ‌— ​Japanese ​logographic ‌and ​syllabic ‌script ​(kanji plus ‌kana ​where ​attested), ​attested ​in ​the ‌classical ​Japanese ‌sources. ​The ‌script ​is ‌written ​top-to-bottom ‌in ​traditional ​contexts ‌and ‌left-to-right ‌in ​modern ​reproductions[^1].

‌The ​scholarly ​transliteration ‌is ​*Amaterasu* ​(Hepburn ‌romanization with ​initial ‌capitalization), ​giving ​the ​normalized ​reading ‌//a.ma.te.ɾa.sɯ//.

‌The ​two ‌characters ​天 ​(ama, ‌heaven) ‌and ‌照 ‌(terasu, ​to ‌illuminate) ​compose ​a ​classic ‌Japanese ​*ateji* ​or ​semantic ‌transcription ​of ​the ​divine name. ‌The ​form ‌天照大神 ​(Amaterasu-ōmikami) ‌is ​the ‌full ‌cult ​title ​used ​in ​ritual ‌and ‌imperial ​sources.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Amaterasu ​is the ‌sun itself ‌made kami. ​Her realm ​is ​Takamagahara, the ​High Plain ​of Heaven, ‌from ​which she ​bestows light ‌and fertility ​upon the ‌world. ​As ancestor ‌of the ​imperial line, ​she also ​guarantees ​political legitimacy: ​the emperor ‌rules as ​her ‌direct descendant. ​Her withdrawal ‌into the ​Heavenly Rock ‌Cave ​(*Ama-no-Iwato*) is ‌the primal ​Shinto myth ​of ‌cosmic crisis ‌and restoration.

‌The domain ​of **Amaterasu** ​is ‌understood within ​the broader ​Japanese religious ‌landscape as ​both ​a specific ‌functional sphere ​and a ‌node ​in a ​network of ​kami, buddhas, ​and local ‌spirits. ‌Shrines, temples, ​and household ‌rites all ​invoke the ​figure ‌in ways ‌that blur ‌strict boundaries ‌between ​Shinto and ‌Buddhist practice[^3]. ​The restoration ​**Amaterasu** therefore ​names ‌not only ​a mythic ​person but ​a ‌living field ​of ritual ​activity: pilgrimage, ​festival, iconography, ‌and ​prayer continue ‌to define ​what the ‌name means ​in ‌contemporary Japan. ‌This combinatory ​or "syncretic" ​context ​is essential ​for interpreting ‌the domains ‌listed above.
​

sources.citation: Breen, John, and Mark Teeuwen, A New History of Shinto (Wiley-Blackwell, 2010).

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
- ​**Mirror** ‌(*Yata ‌no Kagami*) ​— ​one ​of ​the ​three ‌imperial regalia, ​said ​to ‌have ​been ‌used ​to ‌lure her ​from ​the ​cave; ​it ​embodies ‌the sun ​and ‌the ​emperor's ‌divine ​reflection.
‌- **Magatama** ​curved ‌jewel ​— ​another ‌imperial ‌regalia, ‌associated with ​her ​mythic ‌pact.
​- ​**Sword** ‌(*Kusanagi*) — ​recovered ​from ‌the ​tail ‌of ​Yamata no ​Orochi ​by ​Susanō ‌and ‌presented ​to her, ‌later ​passed ​to ‌Ninigi.
‌- ‌**Cock** ‌— the ​crowing ‌bird ​that ​announces ​dawn ‌and marks ​the ​successful ​lure ‌from ​the ​cave.
- ​**Sakaki ‌tree** ​— ‌the ​evergreen ‌(*Cleyera ​japonica*) to ‌which ‌the ​*shide* ​streamers ​were ​fastened during ‌the ‌*kagura* ​dance.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The central ​myth of ‌Amaterasu is ‌the episode of ​the Heavenly ​Rock Cave. ​After Susanō rampaged ​through her ​rice fields ‌and desecrated her ​weaving hall, ​Amaterasu withdrew ‌into a cave ​and sealed ‌it with ​a boulder, plunging ‌the world ​into darkness. ​The eight hundred ​myriad kami ​gathered outside; ​the goddess Ame-no-Uzume ‌performed an ​ecstatic dance ‌on an overturned ​tub, exposing ‌herself and ​making the assembled ‌gods laugh. ​Curious, Amaterasu ‌peeked out; Tajikarao ​seized her ​hand and ‌pulled her into ‌the light. ‌A rope ​(*shimenawa*) was stretched ​before the ‌cave to ​prevent her return. ​The myth ‌establishes *kagura* ​(sacred dance), divination, ​and communal ‌ritual as ​the means ‌by which cosmic ​order is ​restored.

The ​narrative of **Amaterasu** ​participates in ‌the larger ‌mythic program of ​the *Kojiki* ‌and *Nihon ​Shoki*: to explain ​the origins ‌of the ‌imperial house, the ‌division of ‌divine labour, ​and the relationship ‌between the ​human and ​kami worlds. Because ​these chronicles ‌were compiled ​in the eighth ​century under ​imperial patronage, ‌the myths also ​serve a ​political theology, ​grounding earthly authority ‌in divine ​descent and ‌cosmic order[^3]. Read ​comparatively, the ‌story of ​amaterasu illustrates how ‌Japanese myth ‌uses genealogy, ​descent from heaven, ​and the ​negotiation of ​rival domains to ‌construct a ‌coherent sacred ​history.

sections.label: Kojiki & Nihon Shoki
sections.body:
The ​*Kojiki* and ‌*Nihon Shoki* ‌are the ​earliest ​written witnesses ​to **Amaterasu**, ​although ​the figure ‌may have ​circulated in ​oral ‌and local ​cult forms ‌long ​before the ‌eighth century. ​In the ​chronicles, ​Amaterasu appears ​as the ​great ‌august kami ​who illuminates ‌heaven, born ​when ‌Izanagi washed ​his left ‌eye, ​embedded in ‌the imperial ​genealogy and ​the ‌narrative of ‌cosmic order[^1]. ‌The ​*Kojiki* account ​tends to ‌privilege the ​mythic ​lineage leading ‌to Amaterasu ​and ​the imperial ‌house, while ​the *Nihon ‌Shoki* ​often presents ​variant traditions ​side ​by side, ‌preserving conflicting ‌genealogies and ​episodes.

‌Because both ​texts were ​compiled ‌under imperial ‌patronage, their ‌portrayal of ‌Amaterasu ​is never ‌purely "mythological" ​in ​a neutral ​sense; it ‌is also ​a ​statement about ​legitimacy, territory, ‌and ​the proper ​ordering of ​the human ‌and ​divine worlds[^2]. ‌Modern readers ​must ‌therefore distinguish ​between the ‌older narrative ‌strata ​preserved in ​the chronicles ​and ​the ideological ‌framing imposed ‌by the ​compilers.

sections.label: Shinto Sources
sections.body:
Beyond ​the *Kojiki* ‌and ‌*Nihon ​Shoki*, the ​Shinto ​sources for ​**Amaterasu** ​include shrine ‌records ​(*engi*), ​ritual prayers ‌(*norito*), ​imperial ritual ‌protocols, ​and the ‌vast ​corpus ​of local ​festival ​traditions preserved ​at ‌shrines ​across Japan[^1]. ‌These ​documents reveal ‌how ​a figure ‌who ​begins ‌as a ​line ​in an ‌imperial ‌chronicle becomes ‌the ​focus ​of pilgrimage, ‌divination, ​and community ​identity. ‌The ​*Fudoki*, or ​provincial ‌gazetteers, add ​topographical ‌and etymological ​details ​that ​connect Amaterasu ​to ‌specific mountains, ‌rivers, ​and ‌villages.

Medieval ​and ​early-modern Shinto ‌texts ‌also reinterpret ‌Amaterasu ‌in ​light of ‌Buddhist, ​Confucian, and ​nativist ​agendas. The ‌early-modern ​*kokugaku* ​(National Learning) ​scholars, ‌in particular, ​sought ​to ​recover a ‌pure ​Shinto reading ‌of ​the figure, ‌stripped ​of ‌Buddhist accretions[^2]. ‌Their ​interpretations remain ​influential ​in contemporary ​shrine ‌theology ‌and popular ​understanding.

sources.citation: Ono, Sokyo, Shinto: The Kami Way (Tuttle, 1962).
Breen, John, and Mark Teeuwen, A New History of Shinto (Wiley-Blackwell, 2010).

sections.label: Japanese Buddhist Sources
sections.body:
Japanese ​Buddhist ‌sources treat ‌**Amaterasu** ​through ​the lens ​of ​*honji-suijaku*, ​the theory ‌that ​local ​kami are ‌traces ​or ‌manifestations of ​universal ‌Buddhist ​truths. Medieval ​temple-shrine ​complexes ​produced rituals, ​images, ‌and ​narratives ‌that identified ​Amaterasu ‌with ​a Buddhist ‌counterpart, ​integrating ‌the figure ​into ​esoteric ‌mandalas, Pure ‌Land ‌devotion, ​and warrior ​protector ‌cults[^1]. ​These identifications ​were ‌not ​merely symbolic; ​they ‌reorganized ​the ‌ritual calendar, ​patronage ​networks, ​and sacred ​geography ‌of ‌the sites ​involved.

‌The ​Meiji-era policy ​of ‌*shinbutsu ‌bunri* formally ‌separated ‌kami ​and buddhas, ‌but ​Buddhist ​elements survived ​in ‌architecture, ​festival ​customs, and ​popular ‌iconography. ​Modern scholarship ​therefore ​reads ‌Amaterasu through ​both ‌Shinto ​and Buddhist ‌archives, ​recognizing ‌that the ‌two ​traditions ​shaped each ​other ​for ‌more than ‌a ​millennium[^2].

sources.citation: Teeuwen, Mark, and Fabio Rambelli, eds., Buddhas and Kami in Japan (Routledge, 2003).
Sonoda, Minoru, "Shinto and Buddhism," in Shinto in History, ed. Breen and Teeuwen (Curzon, 2000).
